issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette: John, a 74-year-old man of Oceania descent, has been an editor for most of his life. His career had always provided him with a sense of purpose and stability, but over the past few years, it became increasingly difficult for him to find solace in that work due to lingering effects from severe physical abuse by his ex-partner. After their divorce several years ago, John has struggled to cope with the traumatic memories that continue to haunt him. One day at work, a colleague's minor correction triggered an intense emotional reaction within him. The sound of criticism sent waves of fear and discomfort through John’s body, reminiscent of the verbal and physical abuse he endured during his relationship. This triggered memory recall, which was fragmented into vivid snapshots that felt almost alien to him—each moment frozen in time as if it belonged to someone else. John had come to believe that these memories were a form of punishment for who he is—a dehumanized object unable to feel normal emotions. When he recalled the traumatic event, intense rage would surge through him, making it difficult to stay composed at work or in his personal life. These powerful feelings led John to employ various maladaptive strategies such as distraction and avoidance behaviors. He found himself engrossed in crossword puzzles or other mindless tasks whenever a trigger was present, attempting to push away the painful memories. Over time, these triggers became more frequent and intense. For instance, seeing any cues that reminded him of his ex-partner would send John into a state of high alert, forcing him to avoid places where he might encounter such reminders. This avoidance extended to allowing himself to feel strong emotions, as doing so only intensified the memories and their associated pain. John’s negative appraisals further fueled this cycle. He was certain that the trauma had fundamentally changed who he is, making it nearly impossible for him to reclaim his sense of self or feel normal again. The belief that he somehow deserved such treatment because of his character made John question his worth as a person, which in turn influenced how he processed and reacted to memories. The interplay between these elements created a vicious cycle. Whenever a trigger occurred—such as being criticized at work—it would activate the snapshot-like memory recall, intensifying his rage and prompting him to use maladaptive strategies like distraction or emotional numbing. This avoidance behavior then reinforced the idea that he was unable to cope with emotions normally, leading him to further distance himself from any feelings. What frightened John most was how deeply these memories had infiltrated every aspect of his life. He had become increasingly isolated and disconnected from others, fearing another trigger might occur at any moment. The accumulation of these experiences led him to seek help, hoping to regain control over his emotions and reconnect with a sense of normalcy. John’s journey has been marked by the relentless cycle of triggers, memories, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals. He is now seeking professional support to break free from this loop and find ways to navigate his daily life without being overwhelmed by the lingering effects of past trauma.
